summary: Ethernet VPN offers multihoming VPN service across MPLS/IP for connectivity inside a subnet. This document describes an Integrated Routing and Bridging solution built on EVPN for efficient inter-subnet connectivity between tenant systems while keeping EVPN's multihoming capabilities.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes devices in different neighborhoods of a virtual network must talk. This document explains how to connect neighborhoods efficiently without losing backup paths.

questions: what is an irb interface in evpn
subtitle: How EVPN edge routers can both bridge and route tenant traffic locally, without hauling it to a central gateway.

tldr.problem: EVPN connects hosts inside one subnet, but traffic between subnets had to be backhauled to a centralized Layer 3 gateway and back, which is inefficient and sometimes impractical in large multi-tenant data centers.
tldr.mechanism: Each provider edge (PE) router gets Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB): it bridges within a subnet and routes between subnets on a packet-by-packet basis. The RFC defines two modes, symmetric and asymmetric, plus the BGP routes and host-mobility procedures that support them.
tldr.outcome: Inter-subnet traffic is routed at the edge while EVPN's multihoming is kept. Symmetric IRB scales better, asymmetric IRB keeps the control plane simpler, and the operator chooses.

today: RFC 9135 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2021. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Routing Moves to the Edge
sections.content:
EVPN (defined in RFC 7432) gives a multihoming VPN over an MPLS/IP network for intra-subnet connectivity among Tenant Systems (TSs), which can be physical or virtual. Many networks also need inter-subnet connectivity, and doing that through a centralized Layer 3 (L3) gateway means traffic between two subnets on the same PE is backhauled to the gateway and sent back.

RFC 9135 describes an Integrated Routing and Bridging (IRB) solution. A PE with IRB can locally bridge intra-subnet traffic and locally route inter-subnet traffic, packet by packet. The RFC states two requirements. First, each tenant gets IP routing for inter-subnet traffic and Ethernet bridging for intra-subnet and non-routable traffic (non-IP traffic, or IP traffic whose version differs from the version configured in the IP-VRF). Second, IP routing must be switchable off per VLAN on PEs that backhaul that traffic to another PE.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending every letter between buildings to one faraway post office, each building sorts letters for the nearby buildings itself. That is faster and less crowded.

sections.title: The PE Model: MAC-VRFs, IP-VRFs and IRB Interfaces
sections.content:
A tenant that needs IRB on a PE has one IP-VRF plus one or more MAC-VRFs. An IP-VRF is the PE's instance of an IP-VPN; a MAC-VRF is its instance of an EVPN instance (EVI). Each MAC-VRF holds one or more bridge tables, and each bridge table is a VLAN (a broadcast domain). In VLAN-based mode there is one bridge table per MAC-VRF. In VLAN-aware bundle mode there are several.

Each bridge table is connected to the IP-VRF by an L3 IRB interface. Because a tenant subnet is represented by one VLAN, a tenant has as many bridge tables, and as many IRB interfaces, as it has subnets. A receiving PE identifies the bridge table from the MAC-VRF Route Target in VLAN-based mode, but needs both the Route Target and the VLAN ID in VLAN-aware bundle mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighborhood has its own local street map (the bridge table). A small gate connects each street map to one big city map (the IP-VRF), so a letter can go from one neighborhood to another.

sections.title: Symmetric and Asymmetric IRB
sections.content:
The two modes differ in how many lookups each PE does. In symmetric IRB, the ingress PE does a MAC lookup then an IP lookup, and the egress PE does an IP lookup then a MAC lookup. The packet travels between the two IP-VRFs, so the tunnel can be IP-only (for example MPLS or GPE) or an Ethernet NVO tunnel (for example VXLAN). A PE only needs ARP entries for locally connected hosts and bridge tables for locally configured subnets.

In asymmetric IRB, the ingress PE does three lookups (MAC, IP, MAC) and the egress PE does a single MAC lookup. The traffic travels between MAC-VRFs, so the tunnel MUST be of type Ethernet. Each PE MUST keep ARP entries for remote hosts and bridge tables and IRB interfaces for all subnets in an IP-VRF, even subnets with no local hosts, so the RFC asks implementers to consider scale carefully.

The TTL (IPv4) or hop limit (IPv6) is decremented once by the ingress PE in asymmetric IRB, and once by each of the ingress and egress PEs in symmetric IRB. The RFC says the choice between the modes is the operator's, a trade-off between scale (better with symmetric) and control-plane simplicity (better with asymmetric). The modes can coexist: the egress PE signals the mode per host, by a non-zero Label2 and an IP-VRF Route Target (symmetric) or a zero Label2 and no such Route Target (asymmetric).
sections.plainLanguage: In one way of delivering, both post offices do some sorting and the sorting is shared. In the other way, the first post office does almost all the work and the last one just hands the letter over.

sections.title: The Gateway Addresses of an IRB Interface
sections.content:
The PE acts as the default gateway for its attached Tenant Systems. The RFC gives two options. In option 1, all PEs for a tenant subnet use the same anycast gateway IP address and the same anycast MAC address. In option 2, they share the anycast IP address but each uses its own MAC address, and those MACs are aliased to the one IP through the Default Gateway extended community from RFC 7432.

Option 1 is recommended. It is easier to provision, needs no Default Gateway extended community or MAC aliasing, and after a host moves it does not need to refresh its default gateway ARP/ND entry. If applications rely on any form of MAC security, option 1 should be used. If an implementation auto-derives the anycast MAC, it MUST use the ranges defined in RFC 5798: 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID} for IPv4 and 00-00-5E-00-02-{VRID} for IPv6. The VRID is configurable in the range 1 to 255 and defaults to 1. Auto-derivation is only safe when the result cannot collide with a customer MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like giving every building in the complex the same front-desk phone number, so no matter which desk you reach, you get the same helper. A kid who moves buildings does not need a new number.

sections.title: Symmetric IRB: Routes and Forwarding
sections.content:
When a PE learns a host's MAC and IP (for example from an ARP request), it adds them to the bridge table, IP-VRF and ARP table and advertises an EVPN MAC/IP Advertisement route (RT-2). The NLRI Length MUST be 40 (IPv4) or 52 (IPv6). Label2 carries an MPLS label or a VNI for the tenant's IP-VRF. The route MUST carry two Route Targets, one for the MAC-VRF and one for the IP-VRF, and travels with an Encapsulation Extended Community plus, when an Ethernet frame is required, a single EVPN Router's MAC Extended Community. A receiver that sees a non-zero Label2 uses symmetric IRB for that host.

Because not every subnet exists on every PE, PEs MUST also advertise their local subnets as EVPN RT-5 routes. These let a PE send a first packet toward some PE that has the destination subnet, which then probes for the host (gleaning) so the host's MAC and IP get learned and advertised.

On the data path, the ingress PE finds the destination MAC is its own IRB interface MAC, does an IP lookup, decrements TTL, and sends the packet over the tunnel. For an Ethernet NVO tunnel the inner destination MAC is the egress PE's router MAC. The egress PE uses the label or VNI to find the IP-VRF, decrements TTL, looks up the host MAC in its ARP table and forwards into the destination bridge table. The RFC also covers subnets that sit behind a Tenant System, which are advertised as RT-5 routes (RFC 9136) whose next hop is the TS's overlay IP address, resolved recursively to the advertising NVE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each building tells the others which kids live there and what street it is on. To mail a letter, the first mail room puts it in a special envelope addressed to the other mail room, which then walks it to the right kid's door.

sections.title: Asymmetric IRB: Routes and Forwarding
sections.content:
In asymmetric IRB the advertising PE builds the same kind of RT-2 route, but the NLRI Length MUST be 37 (IPv4) or 49 (IPv6), the MPLS Label2 field MUST NOT be included, and the route carries a Tunnel Type Extended Community. The EVPN Router's MAC is not needed, because forwarding uses the destination host's own MAC from the route. The route MUST always carry the MAC-VRF Route Target and MAY also carry an IP-VRF Route Target.

The receiving PE imports the MAC into the MAC-VRF and adds the (IP, MAC) pair to its ARP table or NDP cache. For this to work, all PEs in a tenant's VPN are assumed to be configured with all subnets, even those with no local hosts. A PE that supports only asymmetric IRB and receives a route with a Label2 MUST ignore the Label2 field.

On the data path, the ingress PE does the IP lookup, finds the destination host's MAC in its ARP table, builds the Ethernet frame, and sends it through a regular EVPN Ethernet tunnel. The egress PE only does a MAC lookup, the same as for intra-subnet EVPN forwarding, so all inter-subnet processing is done at the ingress PE.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the first mail room does the hard work. It already knows every kid's exact door, so it writes the final address on the envelope and the last mail room just drops it off.

sections.title: Host Mobility
sections.content:
When a Tenant System moves from a source NVE to a target NVE, IRB needs extra steps on top of the MAC Mobility procedures of RFC 7432. The RFC covers three cases, assuming one IP per MAC: the host sends a gratuitous ARP, the host sends data without an ARP, or the host is silent. NVEs MUST handle at least the first case and SHOULD be able to handle the other two. The text uses IPv4 ARP but says it equally applies to IPv6 ND.

In the gratuitous ARP case, the target NVE updates its tables, notices a MAC move, and advertises an RT-2 with the MAC Mobility extended community and the sequence number incremented by one. The source NVE updates its tables, withdraws its route and sends a local ARP probe to confirm the MAC is gone. Remote NVEs compare sequence numbers and update only if the new one is greater. In the data-only case, the target NVE learns the MAC in the data plane and the source NVE probes for the host. For a silent host, an age-out timer on the source NVE triggers the ARP probe.
sections.plainLanguage: When a kid moves to a new building, the new mail room tells everyone the new address with a higher version number. Old notes with a lower number get ignored.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Layer 2 forwarding follows the security considerations of RFC 7432 for MPLS and RFC 8365 for VXLAN or NVGRE. Layer 3 routing follows RFC 4365, except that this document does not run routing protocols between customer devices and PEs. The RFC calls that a security advantage, since dynamic routing protocols can be blocked on the attachment circuits.

The scheme does not provide confidentiality protection, source authentication, integrity protection or replay protection. Those must come from mechanisms outside the VPN itself. The RFC also notes that an RT-5 route using an Overlay Index depends on an RT-2 route for resolution, so filtering or modifying that RT-2 changes how packets reach the remote subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail rooms do not lock the envelopes. If you need secrecy, you have to add your own lock.
